# Honest DynamoDB usage in this project

There is **zero DynamoDB** in the repo today (no boto3 Dynamo calls, no tables, no docs). boto3 exists only for **SQS** ([relocation_jobs/core/sqs_client.py](relocation_jobs/core/sqs_client.py)).

The product’s real stores, and why that matters:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  panel[Panel_MCP]
  worker[Fetch_worker]
  pg[(Postgres)]
  redis[(Redis)]
  sqs[SQS]
  mem[In_process_dict]

  panel --> pg
  worker --> pg
  panel --> redis
  panel --> sqs
  worker --> mem
  mem -->|"sync_live_to_db"| pg
```

| Store | What it actually holds | Access pattern |
|-------|------------------------|----------------|
| **Postgres** | Catalog, users, tracking, credits ledger, `fetch_runs`, `company_fetch_attempts`, MCP OAuth tokens | Joins, pagination, merge-at-read, audit |
| **Redis** | `countries:labels` hash + generation counter only | Tiny KV; **not** a job queue ([docs/reference/country-cache-redis-hotpath-incident.md](docs/reference/country-cache-redis-hotpath-incident.md)) |
| **SQS** | Opportunity reconcile messages | Work queue ([relocation_jobs/async_jobs/enqueue.py](relocation_jobs/async_jobs/enqueue.py)) |
| **Process memory** | Flask signed-cookie sessions; `_fetch_state` in [relocation_jobs/fetch/state.py](relocation_jobs/fetch/state.py) | Live fetch UI; accurate only in the process that started the run |

[docs/reference/multi-user-scaling-proposal.md](docs/reference/multi-user-scaling-proposal.md) already rejected **NoSQL for catalog/tracking**. That verdict still holds.

## What would be fake (do not add DynamoDB for these)

- **Jobs / companies / board / apply-reject tracking.** The product *is* “load country catalog, merge per-user tracking, bucket, paginate.” That is relational. DynamoDB here is resume padding and would fight [docs/reference/board.md](docs/reference/board.md).
- **Replacing Redis country labels.** Dataset is a handful of keys. The failure mode you already hit was putting network I/O on `all_country_labels()` in a per-company loop — DynamoDB would be the same class of mistake, with higher latency.
- **Replacing SQS.** Queue semantics (retry, DLQ) are already the right AWS primitive.
- **Sessions.** Signed cookies; no server session store.

## What the real usage would be (if you forced one table)

One access pattern in this codebase is already a DynamoDB-shaped item: **fetch live progress**.

- Worker writes progress / activity / capped log often (`sync_live_to_db()` from [relocation_jobs/fetch/runner.py](relocation_jobs/fetch/runner.py)).
- Panel polls `GET /api/fetch/status` (~800ms) and today mixes **in-process dict** with Postgres JSON columns (`activity_log_json`, `log_json`).
- Documented gap: live progress is accurate only in the process that started the fetch ([docs/reference/kafka-fetch-pipeline-proposal.md](docs/reference/kafka-fetch-pipeline-proposal.md)). Production panel and worker are **separate containers**.

Honest table:

- PK: `run_id`
- Attributes: `progress`, `activity`, `log` (capped), `cancel_requested`, `status`
- Writes: UpdateItem from the worker
- Reads: GetItem from the panel poll
- TTL after finalize; **Postgres `fetch_runs` stays the audit source of truth** (that is how the thread-exhaustion incident was diagnosed)

A weaker-but-still-honest second candidate: **MCP OAuth tokens** in [relocation_jobs/mcp/oauth_repo.py](relocation_jobs/mcp/oauth_repo.py) — GetItem by `token_hash`, TTL on `expires_at`, no joins on the hot path. Fine in Postgres at this scale; DynamoDB would be a textbook mapping, not a need.

## Recommendation

**Do not add DynamoDB to kuchup** unless you have a real cross-process live-status problem you want to solve. At `t4g.micro`, one user, ~400 companies, Redis + Postgres already cover KV + relational. Adding a third store to list it on a CV is the thing justDice would probe and fail.

If the interview question is “how would you use DynamoDB here?”: answer with the fetch-live-state table and why the catalog stays on Postgres. That is the real usage. The adjoe/justDice stack (DynamoDB + MySQL at ad-tech scale) maps to **Redis + Postgres at this scale**, not to putting jobs in DynamoDB.

No code changes implied. If you later want a CV-proof implementation, the only honest slice is that one `FetchLiveState` table with TTL — not a catalog migration.

overview: DynamoDB exists for known-key, high-churn lookups at unpredictable scale with stable latency — not as a Postgres replacement. Kuchup does not need it; the only honest local analog is fetch live state (Redis + Postgres already cover that at this scale).
todos: []

# Why people use DynamoDB (then: this project)

People do not pick DynamoDB because it is “AWS NoSQL.” They pick it when the **access pattern is already known** and looks like this:

> I have a key. I need to read or write **that item** very often, at a size I cannot predict, with latency that stays flat as the table grows. I will not join it to five other tables on the way.

That is the product. Everything else is a consequence.

## What DynamoDB is actually good at

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  request[Request]
  pk["Known_key"]
  item[Single_item]
  request --> pk --> item
```

- **GetItem / PutItem by primary key.** Latency stays roughly constant whether the table has 1k or 10B items. Postgres B-trees do not give you that for free at ad-tech scale.
- **Horizontal write scale.** Partition key spreads load. Session stores, shopping carts, player inventory, device↔user maps, ad-auction user state — millions of independent keys, no single hot row if you design the key well.
- **TTL / ephemeral durable state.** Tokens, rate-limit windows, live job progress. Survives process restarts unlike an in-memory dict; cheaper than treating Redis as the source of truth when you already live in AWS.
- **Streams.** Item change → Lambda / another table / archive. Not a queue (that is SQS/Kafka); a change feed.
- **Ops model.** No instance to patch, IAM + VPC, pay per request. That is why Lambda-heavy shops default to it.

Typical real tables (the ones that survive a design review):

- Session / auth token by `token_id` (TTL)
- Shopping cart by `user_id`
- “Current state of X” by `user_id` or `device_id` (game save, ad-user profile, feature flags per tenant)
- Idempotency record by `request_id`
- High-churn status by `job_id` / `run_id`

justDice naming DynamoDB next to ECS/CloudWatch is this world: **per-user or per-request state at mobile-ads scale**, with MySQL/Postgres still holding the relational core. adjoe’s “DynamoDB + MySQL” is the same split.

## What people should not use it for (and often do on resumes)

- Ad-hoc reporting, filters, pagination over a catalog you did not model as a GSIs-for-every-query product
- Many-to-many that you discover later (“also show jobs by city and visa and company”)
- Ledgers, money, anything that wants multi-row integrity as the default
- “We might query it lots of ways” — if you do not know the queries, you want SQL
- A cache in front of Postgres when Redis already exists and the dataset is tiny

Redis vs DynamoDB: both are KV. Redis is **in-memory, microsecond, usually cache or tiny hot state**. DynamoDB is **durable, millisecond, unbounded size**. If the working set fits in RAM and you already run Redis, DynamoDB is the wrong extra box.

## Mapping back to kuchup

# Honest DynamoDB usage in this project

content.text:
People use DynamoDB when they already know the lookup: **I have a key, I need that one item, very often, at a size I cannot predict, and latency should stay flat as the table grows.** They are not using it as “AWS Postgres.”

That access pattern shows up as:

- Session / token by `token_id` (with TTL)
- Cart or “current user state” by `user_id`
- Device ↔ user map, game save, ad-user profile
- Idempotency record by `request_id`
- Live job status by `run_id`

The properties that make those cheaper or safer than a relational table at scale:

- **Get/Put by primary key stays ~constant** whether the table is 1k or 10B items. A B-tree in Postgres does not give you that for free at ad-tech QPS.
- **Writes spread by partition key.** Millions of independent keys, no single bottleneck — as long as you do not create a hot key.
- **Durable without running a box.** Survives deploys; you pay per request. That is why Lambda shops default to it.
- **TTL** for things that should vanish (tokens, live progress).

What it is **not** for: ad-hoc filters, joins, “we might query this lots of ways,” ledgers, a job board. If you do not know the queries yet, you want SQL.

**Redis vs DynamoDB:** both are key-value. Redis is in-memory and tiny/hot. DynamoDB is durable and unbounded. If the data fits in RAM and you already have Redis, DynamoDB is a third store you do not need.

justDice listing DynamoDB next to ECS is the first world: per-user/per-request state at mobile-ads scale, with MySQL still holding the relational core. In kuchup that split is already **Postgres (catalog, tracking, money) + Redis (tiny labels)**. The only DynamoDB-shaped thing here is fetch live progress by `run_id` — and even that is fine in a dict + Postgres JSON at this size.

The interview-useful sentence: DynamoDB is for **known-key, high-churn, scale-unknown lookups**. Postgres is for **relationships you discover by querying**. Mixing those up is how DynamoDB ends up on a CV with no story.
